title: Start tiny
hook: starting absurdly small helps habits begin

segments.voice: Yesterday, habit anchors, and your line was after this, that. Did your anchor come around, and did the new thing ride along? Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

Floss one tooth. Just one. That's the instruction. A dare from a dentist with a sense of humor, maybe. In fact it's one of B. J. Fogg's examples of how to begin a habit, and he means it seriously. One tooth, after brushing, every night. Of course, once the floss is out and wrapped around the fingers, some nights more teeth get done. But the promise was one. The promise was so small it was nearly impossible to break. Today's word turns that small joke into a quiet rule.
screen: `FLOSS ONE TOOTH.` → `NOT A PRANK.` → `A PROMISE TOO SMALL TO BREAK.`

segments.voice: First, too small to skip. Fogg's argument in Tiny Habits is that a new behavior should be so small it takes almost no motivation. On a tired night, a bad day, a day with no time at all, one tooth still gets done. Big plans depend on good days. Tiny ones survive bad ones. Second, the start is the hard part. Getting the floss out, sitting down on the cushion, opening the book: those first moves carry a lot of the friction. A tiny habit is mostly a way of rehearsing the start, over and over, until starting gets easy. Third, an old version of the idea. The Tao Te Ching, in its sixty-fourth chapter, as James Legge translated it, says that a tree too big to wrap your arms around grew from a tiny sprout, a tower of nine stories rose from a small heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand li began with a single step. The same chapter advises dealing with things before they grow. Lao Tzu, as tradition names the author, and a Stanford researcher, far apart in every way, both put the weight on the small beginning. Fourth, grow it later. Tiny isn't the goal. It's the doorway. Fogg says that once a habit is rooted, it can grow on its own, and the extra flossing, the longer sit, comes as a bonus, not a requirement. The rule is only that the floor stays tiny. Thirty seconds on the cushion counts. Some days thirty seconds will turn into ten minutes. Some days it will stay thirty seconds. Both days, the habit holds.
screen: `TOO SMALL TO SKIP.` · `REHEARSING THE START.` · `A TOWER FROM A HEAP OF EARTH.` · then, large: `TINY IS THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: shrink one practice to thirty seconds. Think of a practice you'd like to keep, sitting, reading, a walk, a moment of gratitude, and ask: what's the thirty-second version? Three slow breaths. One line read. Stepping outside and looking at the sky. Now, right here, do it: thirty seconds of just breathing, nothing else expected. Notice how little it asks. Then, since the bell is still holding the time, let the breath keep going, as a bonus, not a requirement. The bell holds the time.
Start tiny. Begin a habit so small it's nearly impossible to skip, and let it grow later. Today's word.
Your line: start tiny. Today, do the thirty-second version of the practice you chose, after your anchor, and count it as done, even if it stays thirty seconds. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: People using the Tiny Habits approach shrink a new habit to a version that takes seconds, like flossing one tooth or one breath of meditation, and let it grow on its own once it's rooted.

what it means: tiny habits survive bad days, and the start is the hard part they practice.

what a scholar hears: Fogg's design keeps the required behavior near zero so motivation barely matters; the Tao Te Ching's chapter sixty-four makes a similar point about tending things while they're small.

notes: Tao Te Ching ch. 64 is paraphrased from Legge's 1891 translation rather than quoted, because the exact Legge wording ('the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step'?) was not certain. Confirm the paraphrase; 'a thousand li' and 'chapter sixty-four' are taken from the text itself.
Confirm Fogg's flossing-one-tooth example and his claim that tiny habits grow naturally once rooted.

Editor pass: Legge's ch. 64 has a tower of nine storeys (now 'nine stories', American spelling), not 'many stories'; the advice to act early comes earlier in the chapter, so 'then' became 'the same chapter'; Lao Tzu is now named 'as tradition names the author'; hook opener varied from day 1289's 'it sounds like a joke'.
